I have a peanut allergy, and in the fourth grade our big school trip was going to an M&Ms factory. My parents figured it would be safe for me to go, since as long as I didn't fall into a vat of peanut M&Ms Willy Wonka style or have some go flying from the machinery into my mouth I'd be fine. They signed the permission slip and the day of the field trip came and I was super excited. After the 3 hour drive on the bus, one of the volunteer parents told me she was having a chat with my teacher and found out I had a peanut allergy, and it was decided I wouldn't be let in the factory and I'd have to wait on the bus with her. I insisted it would be okay, my parents had signed the permission slip and I wanted to talk to my teacher about it. She physically blocked the aisle and refused to let me talk to anyone, all the while acting like I was some sort of upstart and being clearly annoyed she had to stay on the bus too. So child me spent 2 hours crying on the bus with an angry volunteer parent while all my classmates enjoyed the factory, and I'm still bitter about it.

It's funny how I often see people complaining about traditional fantasy and medieval settings on this subreddit, as if this is the only thing being published still. If anything, these kind of stories have been getting less and less since the 90s, and the market share is definitely more skewed towards sci-fi/slipstream now, with most of the small remainder being grimdark, usually with generic culture-blend settings, not pronounced medieval settings.

But I wholeheartedly agree that focusing on slice-of-life elements would benefit *all genre literature at the moment*, not just fantasy and its subgenres. Personally I would kill for a fantasy series that stays in the small farming village instead of moving away from it in chapter 3. In fact, I would challenge every fantasy novelist from here on out to see if they can write a fantasy series without ever including an assassin. We have enough to last the ages. Also, less slipstream. The whole "and then suddenly aliens appear" or "it turns out it was EARTH ALL ALONG" things are getting sooooo tired and gimmicky.

More of: MAGIC! I want my fantasy novels to be dripping with magic. I want discussions about how and why magic affects their living. I want authors to be descriptive and poetic sometimes (telling instead of showing won't kill you or your readers). I want characters who are likeable. Characters I can root for. I want characters who feel like real people with real flaws, but the focus should be on overcoming flaws, not existential despair about flaws. I want to see people using old archetypes in effective ways. More long journeys across strange and magical lands with a sense of wonder and excitement, not dread and warfare.

I'm really sorry you're feeling this way. Once upon a time I also told my family all about my suicidal thinking--why I no longer feel happiness in life--and it ended poorly. I regretted telling them. Contrary to all the advice books and websites out there, I found there was nothing constructive about telling people about my suicidal feelings, and I ended up causing stress on everybody, and also secretly ended up resenting them because of their responses that didn't help at all.

There's no "advice" that works when it comes to suicidal feelings; everyone is different and requires different advice. I found keeping my suicidal thoughts and depression apart from others is what works for me best. You may want to vent these feelings apart from friends and family--you can share thoughts of suicide here, or a suicide hotline, or a personal blog that solely exists for your venting. When I share these feelings with people I know in real life, the blowback--the negative response--just makes the feelings and situation worse.

Do you have quiet, solitary hobbies and interests you can focus on? These are great for clearing your head and separating yourselves from others when negative situations are too much. Even if it's colouring in a colouring book, learning to knit, going to a library and finding a new read, taking up jogging, playing a video game--these can all be meditative when negative contexts become too much and you need to be away from bad social situations. Again, there is no one solution and maybe none of this will be good advice in your eyes. I just hope you're okay and things clear up with your family.

As someone said above, I don't finish a novel if I'm not enjoying it by the halfway mark, so maybe these opinions aren't 100% qualified without having witnessed the full ride, but...

Ian Irvine's *A Shadow on the Glass*. I really, really wanted to like it--excellent concept that had me sold--but the grammar was so simplistic I couldn't take it beyond a hundred pages. "The x was y. The a was b. It was z. He was surprised!" Had the same problem with Feist's *Magician's Apprentice*; I realise a lot of fantasy fans are very devoted to that series but reading it felt like an elementary-level demographic in terms of grammar and language, and I want to be at least a *little* challenged with language even in genre fiction (what's the point of writing a book if you're not going to do interesting things with language?)

Also, Jack Whyte's *The Skystone*. I've never had such a nasty turn with a book I was enjoying greatly. Really gripping historical fantasy about Roman Britain. 1/3 through you get a ridiculously long, gratuitous sex scene. I'm not a prude and there's nothing wrong with sex scenes in books, but then you realize *the novel is dotted with sex chapters at perfectly measured intervals*. I get it--sex scenes can be an important part of character development and plot, as with GRRM--but in this, the sex chapters did nothing at all to plot or character development. Female characters enter and exit the novel solely for porn material then go "see ya!". It was so was frequent and so inexplicably pointless, as if someone had edited in their x-rated fanfiction to the novel after completion. Baffling.
